claims.text: Local chemical inhomogeneities in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles generate microregions with reduced melting thresholds.
Reduced-threshold microregions cause an earlier onset of premelting.
Lower-cohesion regions liquefy first and propagate disorder throughout the nanoparticle, facilitating overall melting.
Synthesis conditions can be varied systematically to produce nanoparticles of the same nominal composition with different degrees of local elemental uniformity.
Chemical ordering and local nanostructure in HEAs depend on thermal processing.
The comparison should use identical heating ramps for compositionally uniform and heterogeneous nanoparticle sets.
Compositional inhomogeneity alters local bonding, charge distribution, or atomic stress in HEAs.
Compositionally inhomogeneous microregions have lower cohesive energy.
Microregions enriched in particular elements liquefy before the rest of the nanoparticle.
Local liquefaction creates disorder that advances a melting front through the nanoparticle.
Greater chemical heterogeneity lowers the overall premelting and melting temperatures relative to a uniform composition.
Chemically heterogeneous particles will begin premelting approximately tens of kelvins earlier than uniform particles.
Chemically heterogeneous particles will exhibit broader and more gradual melting transitions than uniform particles.
Nanoparticles with minimal local compositional gradients will exhibit a higher and more abrupt melting transition aligned with bulk values.
The proposed effect should apply to multi-principal-element nanoparticles that remain single-phase up to moderate temperatures below approximately 1000 K.
The exact upper-temperature limit of the effect depends on composition.
The quantitative shift in premelting onset and the width of the melting range remain experimentally unverified.
A lack of any systematic difference in premelting and melting behavior between compositionally uniform and heterogeneous particles would falsify the hypothesis.
